Future refinements of the LPI 2.0 could include data for other logistics modes.

body_lines.text: Connecting to Compete 2025 introduces the
Logistics Performance Indicators 2.0 (LPI 2.0),
a fundamental redesign of the World Bank’s
former survey-based Logistics Performance
Index toward a system grounded in shipment-
level data. Drawing on large-scale tracking data
from maritime, aviation, and postal operators
—together accounting for over 80 percent of
global goods trade—the LPI 2.0 provide stan
dardized and comparable measures of supply
chain connectivity, speed, and reliability across
economies and over time. The framework com
prises 21 indicators, including 6 core indica
tors capturing direct connectivity and import
time performance in each mode and 15 supple
mentary indicators that shed light on maritime
competition, transshipment dependence, cor
ridor performance for landlocked developing
countries, and postal logistics for e-commerce.
Data for 2023–24 reveal large variations in con
nectivity across regions, substantial time penal
ties associated with transshipment and border
procedures, and high unpredictability concen
trated at ports, transshipment hubs, and inland
checkpoints—particularly for imports and for
landlocked countries. By shifting the focus from
perceptions to observed outcomes, the LPI 2.0
significantly enhance diagnostic precision and
policy relevance, enabling governments to bet
ter prioritize reforms with the highest potential
impact on supply chain connectivity, speed, reli
ability, and resilience.
Logistics underpins the movement of goods
and the operation of supply chains within and
across borders. Efficient logistics reduces trade
costs, connects firms to markets, and supports
development, greatly increasing the volume and
value of trade. Recent disruptions have under
scored that resilient, well-functioning global
logistics networks are essential for growth and
welfare. They help countries withstand shocks,
such as natural disasters, conflict, and technical
failures, by ensuring reliable access to strategic
goods that are too costly or impossible to pro
duce domestically.
The Logistics Performance Indicators 2.0
(LPI 2.0) represent a major methodological
shift toward shipment-level, real-world evidence.
Drawing on large volumes of tracking data
from maritime, aviation, and postal operators
—modes that jointly account for more than
80 percent of the global goods trade—the LPI
2.0 provide standardized indicators of logistics
performance across economies and time. Unlike
the original Logistics Performance Index (LPI),
which was based on surveys of logistics profes
sionals, the LPI 2.0 measure the speed, reliabil
ity, and connectivity of supply chains based on
observed shipment data.
The LPI 2.0’s 21 indicators provide deep in
sight into the functioning of logistics networks.
Six core indicators (one connectivity indicator
and one time indicator for maritime, air, and
postal logistics) and 15 supplementary (connec
tivity and time) indicators provide insights into
maritime competition, transshipment burdens,
corridor performance for landlocked developing
countries (LLDCs), and postal logistics for e-
commerce. Core connectivity indicators capture
the number of countries that can be reached di
rectly via maritime, air cargo, or postal services,
while core time indicators measure import
dwell times and delivery times—key proxies for
logistics efficiency and reliability.
The shift to LPI 2.0 expands coverage, en
hances comparability, and deepens diagnostic
power, enabling policymakers to identify bind
ing constraints with far greater precision. Data
on all 21 indicators are published for 2023 and
2024 at https://lpi.worldbank.org, with op
tions for comparisons across economies and
over time.
Five main findings stand out from the ana
lysis of the LPI 2.0:
There are large connectivity gaps across
and within regions. On average, the Eu
rope and Central Asia region and the North
America region tend to exhibit the strongest
connectivity, depending on the logistics
mode, while Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin
America and the Caribbean lag behind.
These patterns reflect income, geography,
and market accessibility. Within regions,
some developing economies, such as Ma
laysia, Morocco, and Sri Lanka, showcase
stronger performance due to their emer
gence as regional hubs.
Direct connections matter. Roughly half
of containers worldwide require at least one
transshipment. Each transshipment adds
about 18 days to maritime lead times, cre
ating structural disadvantages for small, re
mote economies.
Several low- and middle-income econo
mies clear imported containers within a
few days, which is comparable to high-
income economies, while others experi
ence import dwell times exceeding 10
days. Longer dwell times are due to weak
customs automation, inefficient risk man
agement, and cumbersome inspection and
clearance processes. Aviation dwell times are
shorter than those for containers because
air cargo typically involves smaller volumes,
higher value goods, and more integrated lo
gistics systems.
LLDCs face some of the longest and most
unpredictable import times globally,
with most delays stemming from idling
at ports, border controls, and inland
checkpoints. LLDCs must transit coastal
countries, often crossing multiple borders
and facing complex transit procedures. Cor
ridor lead times and dwell times at the port
of arrival dominate total import time, un
derscoring the importance of regional coor
dination, interoperable transit guarantees,
and streamlined border procedures to im
prove reliability.
Delays are most unpredictable when
goods are stationary—in ports and trans
shipment facilities—and more so for im
ports than exports. Aviation supply chains
show especially high dispersion. Unpredict
ability imposes heavy costs on firms: it dis
rupts production planning, increases inven
tory needs, and reduces competitiveness in
just-in-time and perishable goods markets.
Digital visibility systems, such as those im
plemented in India and the United States,
demonstrate how the value of real-time
tracking can mitigate these risks.
Although logistics services are provided
mainly by private operators, public policy is
fundamental to the performance of global sup
ply and value chains. The LPI 2.0 enable gov
ernments to prioritize interventions with the
highest potential impact on supply chain speed,
reliability, and resilience, tailored to country
circumstances. Policy interventions should be
implemented in a targeted, coherent manner
across three strategic areas:
Enhancing connectivity. Open transport
and logistics markets to competition, invest
in multimodal corridors and logistics clus
ters, and use regional integration and shared
connectivity solutions so smaller or remote
economies can benefit from economies of
scale.
Reducing time and variability. Modernize
border management through digitalization
and risk-based controls (trade facilitation),
improve port and airport performance,
and strengthen traceability to make supply
chains faster and more predictable.
Strengthening institutions and regula
tion. Build a robust governance framework
with transparent public–private partner
ships, competitive logistics markets, and
coordinated policies across ministries, de
partments, and agencies to sustain and scale
logistics reforms.
Logistics consists of a set of activities (freight
transportation, warehousing, brokerage) that
move goods and establish supply chains across
and within borders. Logistics performance
captures the efficiency of supply chain connec
tions, measured in time, cost, and reliability.
Since 2007 the Logistics Performance Index
(LPI) initiative has emphasized the importance
of efficient supply chains in connecting firms to
markets, reducing trade costs, and supporting
development. Logistics performance supports
economic development by enabling trade within
and across borders.
Economics literature, often using the
survey-based LPI, has established that logistics
performance positively and significantly im
pacts the volume and value of bilateral trade,
in particular exports. Logistics influences the
time required for a product to reach its market.
On average, an increase in inland transit time
of one day reduces exports by 7 percent. For
manufactured goods exports the likelihood of
a country exporting to the United States de
creases by 1.5 percent for each additional day of
shipping time.
Logistics inefficiencies hamper economies’
competitiveness because logistics affect manu
facturing firms’ production costs. Improved
logistics performance reduces production costs
and is linked to stronger participation in global
value chains. This is achieved not just through
lower direct logistics costs (transport, storage,
and administrative costs) but also by reducing
the need for inventory and working capital.
A series of disruptions of global logistics
networks in recent years has underlined how
well-functioning logistics networks are essen
tial to production and welfare worldwide.
Resilient logistics networks strengthen econo
mies’ capacity to withstand natural disasters,
conflict, technical failures, or other shocks by
securing reliable access to strategic goods (such
as pharmaceuticals, food, energy, and technolo
gies) that are prohibitively costly to produce do
mestically or cannot be produced at all.
Until 2023 the LPI was based on a survey in
which logistics professionals rated, on a 1–5
scale, the ease of establishing supply chains with
economies they traded with. When the LPI was
conceived in the mid-2000s, perception-based
data were the only option. However, survey-
based indicators have limitations, including per
ception bias and large year-on-year fluctuations.
The Logistics Performance Indicators 2.0
(LPI 2.0) move away from perceptions and rely
instead on objective measures derived from large
volumes of shipment-level tracking data made
available to the World Bank on a confiden
tial basis by global industry and international
tracking initiatives. These data provide granu
lar measures of the speed and connectivity of
international supply chains worldwide. Draw
ing on observations of logistics activity collected
throughout the year, the LPI 2.0 offer a more
comprehensive view of structural performance
and reduce the influence of temporary shocks
or short-lived events on the results.
Three core components define logistics per
formance: time, reliability, and cost. The LPI 2.0
measure time and reliability and capture features
of logistics services that influence costs. They do
so through indicators in two areas: connectiv
ity and time. Connectivity refers to the number
of markets an economy can directly trade with
without having to go through intermediaries
and the number and types of services available.
Time refers to the time that logistics processes
take and their dispersion, which captures the re
liability of the logistics processes. Both connec
tivity and time are measured for different logis
tics modes. Cost is not directly measured by the
LPI 2.0; however, two connectivity indicators
highlight competition within the maritime sec
tor, higher degrees of which tend to be associated
with lower logistics costs.
The 2025 LPI 2.0 cover three logistics
modes—maritime, aviation, and postal—cap
turing over 80 percent of global goods trade by
value. The digitization of global supply chains
means that shipments are now tracked globally
in real time. Though digitization has reached
all transport modes and most logistics services,
tracking data are available in a globally uniform
format only for maritime, aviation, and postal
logistics.
The indicators that make up the LPI 2.0 mea
sure the connectivity and time of international
trade supply chains, including the time ship
ments spend at key nodes such as seaports and
airports. The LPI 2.0 consist of 21 indicators,
each reported at the economy level and with dif
ferent statistical measures.
There are six core indicators in the LPI 2.0, one
connectivity indicator and one time indicator
for each of the three logistics modes covered
(maritime, air, and postal) (table 1.1). The core
maritime connectivity indicator is the number
of unique economies that are reachable from
and that can reach a given economy through
direct maritime services operated by liner ship
ping companies on a predefined rotation.
The core aviation connectivity indicator is the
average number of economies that are reach
able from and that can reach a given economy
through direct cargo-carrying air transport
services. The core postal connectivity indica
tor is the average number of economies with
inbound and outbound postal connections for
parcel and express shipments with a given econ
omy. Parcel and express shipments are primar
ily business-to-business (B2B) transactions and
are thus comparable to maritime container and
air cargo shipments, which are purely B2B.
Connectivity is positively associated with
logistics performance across all modes. More
connected economies can directly reach a larger
number of trade partners and tend to face lower
trade costs. Higher connectivity increases
competition among logistics service provid
ers and encourages investment in trade-related
infrastructure, such as ports and information
technology systems. It is also associated with a
stronger presence of global logistics operators,
which facilitates the diffusion of best practices
and can generate positive spillovers for domestic
logistics services. Connectivity is also critical for
resilience. Economies that rely on only one or a
few international partners are more vulnerable
to disruptions when those links break down,
whether due to natural disasters, conflict, tech
nical failures, or other shocks.
The core time indicators measure the time
it takes to import cargo. The core maritime and
aviation time indicators are container import
dwell time and aviation import dwell time,
respectively. The core postal time indicator is
the business-to-business delivery time, which
captures customs clearance time and the time
until the first attempted or final delivery. Im
port dwell and delivery times were selected as
core indicators because customs procedures are
generally more complex and time-consuming
for imports than for exports, except in econo
mies with strict export controls. In addition, for
air cargo and postal shipments, event tracking is
typically more complete and consistent for im
ports than for exports.
Import dwell and delivery times capture
the efficiency of several components of trade
logistics, including customs clearance and
border management; seaport and airport oper
ations (such as terminal operations, cargo han
dling, and yard management); cargo removal
practices; land transport services (including
the availability of trucks or other equipment for
onward transport); and the quality of transport
and logistics infrastructure.
While the six core indicators provide a solid
overview of an economy’s logistics performance,
the LPI 2.0 provide additional connectivity and
time indicators for maritime and postal logistics
to measure performance more precisely (table
1.2). Two supplementary maritime connectiv
ity indicators—the number of direct container
liner shipping services and alliances servicing
the ports in an economy—highlight competi
tion within the sector, higher degrees of which
tend to be associated with better performance
and lower logistics costs. Three other mari
time indicators gauge how economies could be
affected by their dependence on third-country
shipping hubs. These indicators are maritime
lead time to import from port of arrival to the
destination economy, time spent in transship
ment, and number of transshipments for import
containers. Two indicators that are derived from
empty container movements—export supply
chain initiation and import supply chain termi
nation—reflect logistics efficiency among ship
pers, consignees, and trucking companies.
Two supplementary maritime time indica
tors capture additional aspects of performance
at ports. Turnaround time (twenty-foot equiva
lent unit weighted and unweighted) reflects in
vestment in port capacity and handling equip
ment, as well as the performance of terminal
operations. Container export dwell time re
flects several constraints that differ from those
associated with import dwell time. Controls
applied to export shipments are typically mild
compared with those applied to imports, even in
economies with long import delays. Formalities
such as obtaining certificates of origin, which
are processed upstream, are not automated in
many economies and may delay containers.
Furthermore, export dwell time includes buffer
time, voluntary or mandated by the shipping
lines (such as 48 hours in advance of ship de
parture). Factors such as export-import imbal
ances, distance to port, and frequency of ship
ping connections may influence private sector
strategy and buffer time.
Traders in LLDCs face the challenge that
their shipments usually travel long distances by
land and cross land borders. To capture these
challenges, the LPI 2.0 include four indicators
specific to LLDCs: dwell time at port of arrival
for a container destined for an LLDC, corridor
lead time from port exit to destination, dwell
time at destination (clearance facility in the
LLDC), and reference dwell time at port of ar
rival. A comprehensive measure of container im
port time for LLDCs is the sum of the first three
indicators. The fourth indicator measures import
dwell time for containers destined for the coastal
economy that is typically used as the transit econ
omy for an LLDC. It is a benchmark for dwell
time at port of arrival for a container destined for
an LLDC. Corridor lead time provides informa
tion on road or rail corridor performance.
The supplementary postal logistics indica
tors are similar to the core indicators but focus
on business-to-consumer (B2C) shipments,
which are mostly e-commerce orders. B2C
and B2B shipments typically face different cus
toms procedures. Historically, B2C shipments
(unlike B2B) benefited from de minimis exemp
tions. But in recent years a growing number of
economies have reconsidered these exemptions
and increased scrutiny of B2C shipments, which
has been associated with longer delays.
Since the launch of the LPI in 2007, the rapid
digitization of global supply chains has trans
formed the availability and granularity of logis
tics data. The 2025 LPI 2.0 leverage this shift
by moving beyond perception-based surveys and
drawing on large-scale shipment-level tracking
data obtained under information-sharing agree
ments with global operators. The World Bank
collaborated with international carriers and
data providers to assemble a multimodal data
set covering maritime shipping, air cargo, and
postal services. This approach enables more
objective, timely, and comparable indicators
across economies.
The LPI 2.0 expand coverage relative to ear
lier editions, including many LLDCs and small
island states that were previously excluded due
to data gaps. Coverage remains limited for a
small number of economies affected by embar
goes or severe conflict, where global logistics
operators have little or no presence. The dataset
reflects actual logistics performance along in
ternational supply chains rather than national
averages inferred from surveys.
Maritime indicators draw on several com
plementary sources. Container shipping con
nectivity is derived from MDS Transmodal’s
Containership Databank, which tracks con
tainer vessels and provides detailed information
on service frequency and port rotations. Con
tainer dwell times, lead times, and supply chain
initiation and termination indicators are cal
culated using shipment-level data from a major
global shipping line. Port turnaround times
are based on Automatic Identification System
data from MarineTraffic, which records time
stamped vessel arrivals and departures within
geofenced port areas, enriched with ship and
port registry information.
Aviation and postal indicators complement
the maritime data by capturing time and con
nectivity in high-value and small-parcel trade.
Air cargo indicators are based on data from
Cargo iQ, an International Air Transport
Association interest group, covering airport-
to-airport shipments across more than 180
economies. Postal indicators rely on electronic
tracking records from the Universal Postal
Union, covering billions of international postal
items annually and providing end-to-end time
stamps from posting to final delivery.
Together, these datasets form the empirical
backbone of the LPI 2.0, enabling a more gran
ular and evidence-based assessment of logistics
performance across economies and modes.
This chapter presents high-level findings from
the Logistics Performance Indicators 2.0 (LPI
2.0) with a focus on systematic patterns across
regions and income groups. Data on all 21
indicators for 2023 and 2024 are published
at https://lpi.worldbank.org, with options for
comparisons across economies and over time.
On average, the Europe and Central Asia region
and the North America region tend to have the
highest connectivity across logistics modes,
while the Latin America and the Caribbean
region and the Sub-Saharan Africa region tend
to have the lowest, depending on the mode con
sidered (figure 2.1, panels a, b, c), although some
developing economies perform strongly. This
pattern mirrors broader income and geographic
differences: high-income economies are gen
erally more connected than low- and middle-
income economies (figure 2.1, panels d, e, f). The
connectivity indicators also reflect an economy’s
position in the global shipping network and its
proximity to centers of economic activity.
Developing economies that have emerged as
regional or global shipping hubs, such as Malay
sia, Morocco, and Sri Lanka, have much higher
connectivity than their neighbors with the same
accessibility. For the same level of market acces
sibility, larger economies have more connections
—for instance, Australia and New Zealand,
which are among the economies with the low
est accessibility, have the highest connectivity at
that level of accessibility (figure 2.2).
Connectivity increased during 2023–24
across most regions. Between 2023 and 2024
the number of direct liner shipping, aviation,
and postal services connections increased across
most income groups and regions, though some
economies in South Asia and in the Middle East
and North Africa showed a small decline (see
figure 2.1). These declines in maritime connec
tivity occurred largely because of the Red Sea
crisis.
The existence of direct maritime connec
tions matters because it removes significant
delays associated with transshipments. Though
about half of containers travel directly to their
destination, the rest may be transshipped mul
tiple times—up to eight in some cases (figure
2.3, panel a). Small island states are the most
affected, with several averaging more than two
transshipments in 2024: São Tomé and Príncipe
(2.6), Anguilla (2.4), the Comoros (2.4), and St.
Kitts and Nevis (2.2). Each transshipment adds
to maritime lead times—roughly 18 extra days
per transfer—underscoring the heavy burden
of hub dependence for these economies (figure
2.3, panel b). But the hub and spoke structure
of modern long-distance supply chains, where
smaller freight loads are consolidated into larger
ones at hubs using high-capacity equipment, has
proven cost-effective for carriers while providing
small and peripheral economies with access to
global routes.
Several low- and middle-income economies have
moderate container import dwell times, similar
to those in high-income economies, but many
have exceptionally long ones (more than two
weeks). Most of the economies with excessive
dwell time are in Sub-Saharan Africa and in the
Middle East and North Africa. Aviation import
dwell time is typically only half of container
import dwell time or less (figure 2.4). This dif
ference reflects the smaller volume, smaller size,
and higher value of air cargo compared with
maritime cargo. Air cargo operations are more
tightly integrated with door-to-door logistics
chains, and a share of shipments is cleared by
customs before arrival, whereas maritime cargo
is usually cleared after arrival. Underperforming
economies overlap between the two indicators.
The economies with the shortest dwell times are
typically active air cargo hubs, such as Belgium,
the Netherlands, and Singapore.
Long container import dwell times often re
flect inefficient processes for clearing imported
goods. Poor performance may stem from lim
ited automation in customs clearance and port
logistics—areas that port community systems
can help improve. Inadequate risk manage
ment and inefficient inspection practices by
customs officials can also lengthen dwell times.
Other requirements, including foreign exchange
controls and inspections by agencies beyond
customs, may further add to delays. Importer
behavior can also contribute—for example,
when importers use ports for storage.
Business-to-business (B2B) postal delivery
time is highly dispersed across low- and lower-
middle-income economies. While this pattern is
common to other logistics modes, underperform
ing economies differ somewhat across modes. The
economies with the longest container and avia
tion import dwell times are concentrated in Sub-
Saharan Africa, whereas long B2B postal delivery
times are more common in Latin America and
the Caribbean and in Sub-Saharan Africa.
The differences between postal logistics per
formance and that of maritime containers and air
cargo partly reflect the distinct facilities and pro
cesses involved in handling these different types
of shipments. Two factors are especially impor
tant. First, geography and domestic distribution
matter: The postal indicator includes both the
time spent at the postal bureau of entry and the
time until delivery, which can be prolonged when
domestic postal networks are not optimized, par
ticularly in geographically large economies. Sec
ond, customs clearance practices play a key role.
In some economies, including several in Latin
America and the Caribbean, inbound shipment
information is not electronically linked to cus
toms systems, so clearance relies on paper docu
mentation for each shipment, increasing delays.
Landlocked developing countries (LLDCs) are
among the most logistically constrained coun
tries because their cargo needs to transit through
coastal countries, crossing more than one bor
der. As a result, the time to import a container
is exceptionally long and uneven for LLDCs.
Among the three components of time to import
for LLDCs, corridor lead time and dwell time
at port of arrival in coastal country tend to be
the largest, followed by dwell time at destination
(figure 2.5). In addition, dwell time at the port
of arrival is longer for goods in transit than for
goods destined for coastal countries.
The long import times are not explained by
corridor distance but by the considerable time
cargo spends idling at ports, at borders, and in
checkpoints along transit corridors en route to
the LLDCs—reinforcing the importance of
pursuing corridor reforms. These reforms in
clude tackling border crossing delays, improving
exchange of information on transit vehicles and
goods across borders, and adopting better transit
procedures and guarantee mechanisms. Among
the biggest technical challenges is cross-border
interoperability of financial guarantees or bonds
covering the customs value of goods in transit.
The best practice systems are the Transports In
ternationaux Routiers system (managed by the
International Road Union and used in Central
Asia and the Balkans) and the Common Transit
procedure (applicable to European Union and
European Free Trade Association countries). Ex
cept for the Secretary of Economic Integration
of Central America transit system, these systems
have not been fully adopted by other regions.
The highest dispersion of dwell, delivery, and
lead times occurs when goods are not in motion:
in ports, border controls, and inland check
points. The LPI 2.0 assess supply chain reli
ability at the economy level through the inter
quartile range of dwell, delivery, and lead times
(figure 2.6). Dispersion increases with median
dwell times and is, on average, 36 percent higher
for imports than for exports (figure 2.7). Dis
persion is even higher for aviation supply chains.
In well-functioning ports with seamless
clearance systems, processing an unloaded con
tainer starts immediately. In Le Havre (France)
10 percent of containers leave the port in 1 day
or less, 50 percent do so in 3.8 days or less, and
only 25 percent take more than 5.9 days (figure
2.8). By contrast, in many ports only a few con
tainers are cleared during the first few days after
arrival. In Apapa (Nigeria) only 0.2 percent of
containers leave the port in 1 day or less, 50 per
cent do so in 13.4 days or less, and 25 percent
take more than 22.1 days, and in Algiers (Alge
ria), only 0.1 percent leave the port in 1 day or
less, 50 percent do so in 17.6 days, and 25 per
cent take more than 26.3 days.
Dispersion reflects the unpredictability of
port clearance processes and port operations,
with adverse implications for supply and value
chains. Unreliable control processes, especially
for clearing imported goods, are associated with
the complexity of the processes, which often re
quire collecting paper documentation and com
plying with complicated foreign exchange regu
lations. With export dwell time, factors include
operational constraints, such as slot availability,
service frequency, and, in some economies, ex
port clearances. Variations in shipper productiv
ity and behavior can also affect the dispersion of
export and import dwell time. The cost of unre
liability can be substantial for firms’ inventories
and operational planning, especially in just-in-
time supply chains and those handling perish
able goods.
Tracking goods with information technol
ogy platforms, known as supply chain visibility,
helps firms hedge some of the consequences of
unreliability. Technology can help firms better
anticipate the next steps in the supply chain.
Examples of recent large-scale visibility system
include the Freight Logistics Optimization
Works (FLOW) initiative in the United States
and the Unified Logistics Information Platform
in India.
In some low- and middle-income economies
container ships spend an excessive time at port
(figure 2.9, panel a). Port turnaround time
reflects port handling capacity and productiv
ity and is more directly shaped by infrastructure
capacity and terminal management practices
than by trade facilitation measures. In most
upper-middle- and high-income economies the
average weighted turnaround time is less than
two days, compared with two to six days in sev
eral low- and lower-middle-income economies.
These differences point to substantial scope
for improving container port performance in
low- and lower-middle-income economies.
For most countries, however, the most
painful frictions are in trade facilitation and
land-side logistics. This is evidenced by ship
turnaround time typically being much shorter
than container import dwell time (figure 2.9,
panel b). Though dwell time is influenced by
infrastructure, it captures primarily the perfor
mance of customs and other border procedures
and therefore depends largely on trade facilita
tion policies.
Strong B2B and business-to-consumer
(B2C) postal logistics performance is critical
for e-commerce and SME participation. Al
though standard postal services experienced
considerable market erosion in 2023 and 2024,
they continue to play a substantial role in the
last-mile delivery of cross-border e-commerce
shipments (B2C), with close to 40 percent
of these items being delivered by traditional
postal services in 2024. Poor postal logistics
performance tends to constrain small and me
dium enterprises (SMEs) from participating in
e-commerce, with B2C SMEs usually finding it
harder to scale up than B2B SMEs because B2C
business entails a higher intensity of shipping.
Furthermore, B2C postal delivery times tend
to be longer than B2B delivery times, primar
ily in lower-middle-income economies, pointing
to inconsistencies in postal logistics that penal
ize firms engaged in B2C e-commerce in these
economies (figure 2.10).
Logistics services—such as freight transporta
tion, warehousing, and brokerage—are deliv
ered primarily by private firms. But their effi
ciency and the overall performance of supply
chains are fundamentally shaped by public
policy. Logistics operations depend on publicly
funded infrastructure, must comply with border
controls managed by state agencies, and operate
within fiscal, environmental, safety, and compe
tition regulations set by governments.
Policy interventions to improve logistics per
formance, as measured by the LPI 2.0, should
be implemented in a targeted, coherent manner
across three strategic areas:
Enhancing connectivity through strategic
investment and liberalization.
Reducing time and variability through trade
facilitation and infrastructure.
Strengthening the institutional and regula
tory environment for logistics.
Together with reforms to reduce logistics
costs—which are not directly measured by the
LPI 2.0—these areas provide a practical policy
agenda for governments seeking to improve lo
gistics performance.
A country’s connectivity to global production
and distribution networks is determined by its
physical geography, the quality and reach of its
transport infrastructure, and the network strate
gies of international operators. While geography
is fixed, public policy can greatly influence how
well a country is connected to global markets.
Governments can act on three main fronts.
1.1 Liberalizing markets for transport and
logistics services. Policies that open markets
to competition and foreign participation can
encourage international operators to expand
their networks and increase the number of part
ner economies served. Examples include:
Liberalizing maritime services and port op
erations to attract global shipping lines and
terminal operators.
Adopting “Open Skies” agreements in avia
tion to allow more carriers, routes, and fre
quencies.
Removing restrictive regulations that limit
entry or capacity in key logistics services
(e.g., freight forwarding, express delivery).
These measures can increase service fre
quency, reduce costs, and improve the reliability
of international connections.
1.2 Developing hubs, corridors, and logis
tics clusters. Governments can use infrastruc
ture planning and spatial policies to position
their economies as attractive nodes in regional
and global networks. This involves:
Investing in and upgrading gateway ports,
airports, and dry ports that can serve as re
gional hubs.
Developing multimodal transport corridors
that connect these gateways to major pro
duction and consumption centers.
Promoting logistics and industrial clusters
around key hubs through zoning, serviced
land, and streamlined permitting.
These policies can help transform a coun
try’s connectivity and establish it as a regional
logistics and manufacturing hub.
1.3 Pursuing regional integration and
shared connectivity solutions. For small,
landlocked, or remote economies, national
policies alone may not be sufficient to achieve
scale. Regional cooperation becomes essential.
Key governments include:
Harmonizing regulations and technical
standards with partner economies to facili
tate cross-border transport and logistics.
Developing regional transit regimes and
corridor management institutions to ensure
seamless movement of goods.
Coordinating investment in regional gate
ways and corridors so that smaller econo
mies can “piggyback” on the trade flows
of larger neighbors and global distribution
centers.
By pursuing these policies, governments
can systematically improve their connectivity
performance, making their economies more
attractive for trade and participation in global
value chains.
Time-related indicators—such as dwell time
in ports and airports, ship turnaround time,
and postal delivery time—are more respon
sive to policy than connectivity indicators
are. Reducing delays and variability is criti
cal for modern supply chains, especially those
integrated into just-in-time production and
e-commerce.
Governments can influence time and reli
ability through three main sets of policies.
2.1 Modernizing border management and
trade facilitation. Border procedures are often
a major source of delays and uncertainty. Key
reforms include:
Implementing risk-based management sys
tems to focus inspections on high-risk con
signments and expedite low-risk trade.
Digitizing customs and border processes,
including electronic submission of docu
ments, prearrival processing, and electronic
payment of duties and fees.
Establishing coordinated border manage
ment, where customs and other border agen
cies (e.g., health, agriculture, security) align
procedures and share information.
For landlocked countries, designing and
implementing efficient transit regimes, in
cluding transit guarantees, bonded trans
port, and streamlined procedures at border
crossings.
These measures can greatly reduce import
and export dwell times and improve the predict
ability of clearance processes.
2.2 Improving gateway efficiency and ter
minal operations. Even when border proce
dures are efficient, poor performance at ports,
airports, and inland terminals can create bottle
necks. Government actions can include:
Investing in infrastructure to address ca
pacity constraints, such as berth extensions,
yard expansion, and improved access roads
and rail links.
Promoting operational improvements, in
cluding port community systems, electronic
appointment systems for truck arrivals, per
formance-based contracts with terminal op
erators, and efficient pricing of port storage.
Using public–private partnerships (PPPs) to
bring in private expertise and capital for ter
minal management, with clear performance
targets for productivity and service quality.
These policies directly affect ship turn
around time, container dwell time, and the reli
ability of gateway operations.
2.3 Enhancing supply chain traceability and
predictability. For firms participating in global
value chains, predictability is often as important
as speed. Governments can support more pre
dictable logistics by:
Addressing upstream causes of delays, such
as complex banking procedures for foreign
exchange, documentation requirements, or
licensing processes that hold up shipments
before they reach customs.
Encouraging the use of digital tracking and
tracing systems, including integration of
customs, port, and logistics operator (in
cluding postal services) data.
Supporting the development of express lo
gistics and time-definite delivery services,
which rely on streamlined customs proce
dures and integrated handling at gateways.
By focusing on both the direct and indirect
sources of delay, governments can save time, re
duce variability, and improve the reliability of
supply chains.
Physical investments and trade facilitation
reforms are most effective when supported by
a sound institutional and regulatory environ
ment. This area focuses on how governments
organize, regulate, and coordinate the logistics
sector. Governments can do so in three key pol
icy areas.
3.1 Leveraging public–private partner
ships and improving sector governance.
PPPs, when well designed and embedded in a
clear policy framework, can be powerful tools
to improve logistics performance. Governments
should consider:
Using PPPs for port, airport, and inland
terminal operations where private opera
tors can bring management expertise, tech
nology, and investment.
Defining transparent concession frame
works with measurable performance indi
cators (e.g., crane productivity, truck turn
around time, dwell time) and mechanisms
for monitoring and enforcement.
Ensuring that PPPs are aligned with broader
logistics and trade strategies rather than ne
gotiated as isolated deals.
3.2 Strengthening competition, market
structure, and supporting domestic logistics
development. A competitive and professional
logistics services market is essential for efficient
supply chains. Policy priorities include:
Removing unnecessary barriers to entry
and anticompetitive regulations in truck
ing, freight forwarding, warehousing, and
express delivery.
Modernizing trucking regulations (e.g., axle
load limits, vehicle standards, licensing) to
balance safety and environmental objectives
with efficiency.
Opening markets to private and foreign pro
viders where appropriate, while ensuring a
level playing field and effective competition
oversight.
Supporting the development of higher
value-added logistics services (e.g., third-
party logistics, contract logistics, cold chain)
through clear regulations and investment-
friendly policies.
These measures help improve domestic lo
gistics performance and enable firms to access
more sophisticated services, which in turn sup
ports better connectivity and shorter delivery
times.
3.3 Enhancing policy consistency, coordi
nation, and implementation capacity. Con
nectivity and logistics performance improve
gradually as operators adjust their networks and
investment. Governments therefore need:
Stable, predictable policy frameworks that
give investors confidence to commit capital
to infrastructure and logistics services.
Institutional mechanisms—such as national
logistics councils or trade facilitation com
mittees—to coordinate across ministries
(transport, trade, finance, customs, indus
try) and with the private sector.
Clear national logistics or trade facilitation
strategies with measurable targets linked to
key performance indicators, such as those in
the LPI 2.0, and systems to monitor prog
ress and adjust policies as needed.
Strengthened implementation capacity in
customs, port authorities, transport agen
cies, and other relevant institutions, includ
ing training, change management, and ad
equate resourcing.
A coherent institutional and regulatory en
vironment ensures that reforms under the first
two areas are sustained and that their benefits
are fully realized.
Logistics reform is not a one-size-fits-all
endeavor. Economies differ in geography, eco
nomic structure, institutional capacity, and
political economy. The LPI 2.0 provides a struc
tured way to diagnose performance gaps in
connectivity and time and to link those gaps to
specific policy levers.
By organizing interventions under three
areas—enhancing connectivity, reducing time
and variability, and strengthening institutions
and regulations—governments can:
Identify the root causes of logistics frictions.
Prioritize the reforms with the highest ex
pected impact on supply chain performance
and trade outcomes.
Sequence interventions in a way that re
flects their capacity and socio-political
context.
Ultimately, the value of the LPI 2.0 lies not
only in measuring logistics performance but
also in guiding governments toward concrete,
evidence-based policy actions that improve
connectivity, reduce time to trade, and sup
port integration into regional and global value
chains.
